fp2_hyperbolic_exponential.description: Use the exponential definitions of sinh, cosh and tanh, and solve exact equations in a positive exponential.

sections.title: What do the exponential definitions mean?
sections.label: The three definitions
sections.intro: Treat \(\mathrm e^x\) and \(\mathrm e^{-x}\) as reciprocal positive numbers. Their difference supplies the odd function and their sum supplies the even one.

blocks.html: \(\sinh x=\frac{\mathrm e^x-\mathrm e^{-x}}{2}\), \(\cosh x=\frac{\mathrm e^x+\mathrm e^{-x}}{2}\) and \(\tanh x=\frac{\sinh x}{\cosh x}\). At zero these give \(0,1,0\). A value such as \(\mathrm e^x=4\) is enough to evaluate all three exactly.
Forgetting the factor \(\frac12\) in both definitions doubles both values. It cancels only after forming the quotient.
Use \(\cosh x+\sinh x=\mathrm e^x\) as a quick check on any pair of values.

blocks.title: Half a difference and half a sum
blocks.prompt: Given \(\mathrm e^x=4\), give the exact values of \(\sinh x\) and \(\cosh x\).
blocks.hint: Use the exponential definitions and keep the exponential strictly positive.
blocks.solution:
The reciprocal exponential is \(\mathrm e^{-x}=\frac{1}{4}\).

Half their difference gives \(\frac{15}{8}\) and half their sum gives \(\frac{17}{8}\). Using the two definitions preserves the sign of the sine.

blocks.title: Keep the sign of the difference
blocks.prompt: Given \(\mathrm e^x=\frac{3}{5}\), give the exact values of \(\sinh x\) and \(\cosh x\).
blocks.hint: Use the exponential definitions and keep the exponential strictly positive.
blocks.solution:
The reciprocal exponential is \(\mathrm e^{-x}=\frac{5}{3}\).

Half their difference gives \(-\frac{8}{15}\) and half their sum gives \(\frac{17}{15}\). Using the two definitions preserves the sign of the sine.

sections.title: Why is the tangent always between −1 and 1?
sections.label: Hyperbolic tangent
sections.intro: Divide the difference by the sum. Multiplying numerator and denominator by \(\mathrm e^x\) gives an expression in a single positive variable.

blocks.html: \(\tanh x=\frac{\mathrm e^{2x}-1}{\mathrm e^{2x}+1}\). The difference is smaller in magnitude than the sum of two positive terms. This also explains why neither endpoint of the range is attained.
Subtracting one from \(\mathrm e^{2x}\) can make the numerator negative. The denominator stays positive.
Write the denominator explicitly when arguing about sign or range.

blocks.title: Read the sign from the quotient
blocks.prompt: Given \(\mathrm e^x=3\), find \(\tanh x\) exactly and state its sign.
blocks.hint: Use the exponential definitions and keep the exponential strictly positive.
blocks.solution:
\(\tanh x=\frac{\mathrm e^{2x}-1}{\mathrm e^{2x}+1}\) is the quotient of the exponential forms.

Use \(\mathrm e^{2x}=9\). The denominator is positive, so it cannot reverse the sign. Substitution gives \(\frac{4}{5}\).

sections.title: Where do the reciprocal functions exist?
sections.label: Three reciprocals
sections.intro: Once the values of sine and cosine are known, take their reciprocals and the reciprocal of their quotient. A zero of the original function becomes an excluded input.

blocks.html: \(\operatorname{sech}x=\frac1{\cosh x}\) exists everywhere. \(\operatorname{cosech}x=\frac1{\sinh x}\) and \(\coth x=\frac{\cosh x}{\sinh x}\) exclude \(x=0\). Their sign changes across that exclusion.
A reciprocal such as \(\operatorname{sech}x\) is different from the inverse function \(\cosh^{-1}x\). One flips the output and the other reverses the map.
State the exclusion before simplifying an expression containing \(\operatorname{cosech}x\).

blocks.title: Use a reciprocal with x below zero
blocks.prompt: Given \(\mathrm e^x=\frac{2}{5}\), calculate \(\operatorname{sech}x\) and \(\operatorname{cosech}x\).
blocks.hint: Use the exponential definitions and keep the exponential strictly positive.
blocks.solution:
From the exponential definitions \(\cosh x=\frac{29}{20}\) and \(\sinh x=-\frac{21}{20}\).

Take reciprocals after evaluating. The hyperbolic secant is positive, and the sign of the hyperbolic cosecant agrees with the sign of the sine.

blocks.title: Use two positive reciprocals
blocks.prompt: Given \(\mathrm e^x=6\), calculate \(\operatorname{sech}x\) and \(\operatorname{cosech}x\).
blocks.hint: Use the exponential definitions and keep the exponential strictly positive.
blocks.solution:
From the exponential definitions \(\cosh x=\frac{37}{12}\) and \(\sinh x=\frac{35}{12}\).

Take reciprocals after evaluating. The hyperbolic secant is positive, and the sign of the hyperbolic cosecant agrees with the sign of the sine.

sections.title: How do I solve an equation in exponentials?
sections.label: Replace the exponential
sections.intro: Changing variables to \(T=\mathrm e^x\) turns expressions in \(\mathrm e^x\) and \(\mathrm e^{-x}\) into rational expressions in \(T\). The transformed variable has a fixed restriction.

blocks.html: Write \(T>0\) first. Multiplying by \(T\) is then reversible. Solve the resulting equation in \(T\), remove non-positive roots and finally use \(x=\ln T\).
A negative algebraic root can satisfy the quadratic while giving no real value of \(x\). Taking the logarithm of its magnitude changes the equation.
If both roots are positive, report both logarithms.

blocks.title: Discard the negative root
blocks.prompt: Given \(\sinh x=\frac{21}{20}\), find the only positive value of \(\mathrm e^x\) that can give this result.
blocks.hint: Use the exponential definitions and keep the exponential strictly positive.
blocks.solution:
Write \(T=\mathrm e^x>0\) in the sine definition. Then \(T^2-2(\sinh x)T-1=0\).

The roots have product \(-1\). They are \(\frac{5}{2}\) and \(-\frac{2}{5}\) here. Only \(\frac{5}{2}\) is permitted.

sections.title: When is it quicker to square the exponential?
sections.label: Choose the substitution
sections.intro: A quotient for \(\tanh x\) contains only \(\mathrm e^{2x}\) after simplification. Substituting \(U=\mathrm e^{2x}\) makes it a linear equation in \(U\).

blocks.html: For \(\tanh x=k\), obtain \((1-k)U=1+k\). State \(-1
With \(U=\mathrm e^{2x}\), using \(x=\ln U\) gives twice the required value.
Check the sign of \(x\) against the sign of the hyperbolic tangent.

blocks.title: Choose the square root of U
blocks.prompt: Let \(w=\tanh^{-1}\left(\frac{7}{25}\right)\). Give \(\mathrm e^w\) exactly and identify the sign of \(w\).
blocks.hint: Use the principal domain where the original hyperbolic function has an inverse.
blocks.solution:
From the tangent definition, \(T^2=\frac{1+\tanh w}{1-\tanh w}\). Use the positive square root for \(T\).

Solving gives \(T=\frac{4}{3}\). The logarithm of \(T\) is positive.

examples.title: Evaluate using a positive exponent
examples.question: Given \(\mathrm e^x=3\), give the exact values of \(\sinh x\) and \(\cosh x\).
solution: The reciprocal exponential is \(\mathrm e^{-x}=\frac{1}{3}\).
Half their difference gives \(\frac{4}{3}\) and half their sum gives \(\frac{5}{3}\). Using the two definitions preserves the sign of the sine.

examples.title: Evaluate below zero
examples.question: Given \(\mathrm e^x=\frac{2}{3}\), give the exact values of \(\sinh x\) and \(\cosh x\).
solution: The reciprocal exponential is \(\mathrm e^{-x}=\frac{3}{2}\).
Half their difference gives \(-\frac{5}{12}\) and half their sum gives \(\frac{13}{12}\). Using the two definitions preserves the sign of the sine.

examples.title: Simplify the quotient before substituting
examples.question: Given \(\mathrm e^x=4\), find \(\tanh x\) exactly and state its sign.
solution: \(\tanh x=\frac{\mathrm e^{2x}-1}{\mathrm e^{2x}+1}\) is the quotient of the exponential forms.
Use \(\mathrm e^{2x}=16\). The denominator is positive, so it cannot reverse the sign. Substitution gives \(\frac{15}{17}\).

examples.title: Reciprocals of a negative-input pair
examples.question: Given \(\mathrm e^x=\frac{1}{2}\), calculate \(\operatorname{sech}x\) and \(\operatorname{cosech}x\).
solution: From the exponential definitions \(\cosh x=\frac{5}{4}\) and \(\sinh x=-\frac{3}{4}\).
Take reciprocals after evaluating. The hyperbolic secant is positive, and the sign of the hyperbolic cosecant agrees with the sign of the sine.

examples.title: Reciprocals at a positive input
examples.question: Given \(\mathrm e^x=5\), calculate \(\operatorname{sech}x\) and \(\operatorname{cosech}x\).
solution: From the exponential definitions \(\cosh x=\frac{13}{5}\) and \(\sinh x=\frac{12}{5}\).
Take reciprocals after evaluating. The hyperbolic secant is positive, and the sign of the hyperbolic cosecant agrees with the sign of the sine.

examples.title: Retain the admissible exponential
examples.question: Given \(\sinh x=\frac{3}{4}\), find the only positive value of \(\mathrm e^x\) that can give this result.
solution: Write \(T=\mathrm e^x>0\) in the sine definition. Then \(T^2-2(\sinh x)T-1=0\).
The roots have product \(-1\). They are \(2\) and \(-\frac{1}{2}\) here. Only \(2\) is permitted.

examples.title: Recover the exponent from a tangent value
examples.question: Let \(w=\tanh^{-1}\left(\frac{5}{13}\right)\). Give \(\mathrm e^w\) exactly and identify the sign of \(w\).
solution: From the tangent definition, \(T^2=\frac{1+\tanh w}{1-\tanh w}\). Use the positive square root for \(T\).
Solving gives \(T=\frac{3}{2}\). The logarithm of \(T\) is positive.
In logarithmic form this evaluation is \(w=\ln\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)\). The argument is positive as required.

extraPractice.title: Calculate directly
extraPractice.prompt: Given \(\mathrm e^x=7\), give the exact values of \(\sinh x\) and \(\cosh x\).
extraPractice.hint: Use the exponential definitions and keep the exponential strictly positive.
extraPractice.solution:
The reciprocal exponential is \(\mathrm e^{-x}=\frac{1}{7}\).

Half their difference gives \(\frac{24}{7}\) and half their sum gives \(\frac{25}{7}\). Using the two definitions preserves the sign of the sine.

extraPractice.title: Simplify a negative quotient
extraPractice.prompt: Given \(\mathrm e^x=\frac{2}{7}\), find \(\tanh x\) exactly and state its sign.
extraPractice.hint: Use the exponential definitions and keep the exponential strictly positive.
extraPractice.solution:
\(\tanh x=\frac{\mathrm e^{2x}-1}{\mathrm e^{2x}+1}\) is the quotient of the exponential forms.

Use \(\mathrm e^{2x}=\frac{4}{49}\). The denominator is positive, so it cannot reverse the sign. Substitution gives \(-\frac{45}{53}\).

extraPractice.title: Compare signs before calculating
extraPractice.prompt: Given \(\mathrm e^x=\frac{3}{7}\), calculate \(\operatorname{sech}x\) and \(\operatorname{cosech}x\).
extraPractice.hint: Use the exponential definitions and keep the exponential strictly positive.
extraPractice.solution:
From the exponential definitions \(\cosh x=\frac{29}{21}\) and \(\sinh x=-\frac{20}{21}\).

Take reciprocals after evaluating. The hyperbolic secant is positive, and the sign of the hyperbolic cosecant agrees with the sign of the sine.

extraPractice.title: Find the only positive exponential
extraPractice.prompt: Given \(\sinh x=-\frac{33}{56}\), find the only positive value of \(\mathrm e^x\) that can give this result.
extraPractice.hint: Use the exponential definitions and keep the exponential strictly positive.
extraPractice.solution:
Write \(T=\mathrm e^x>0\) in the sine definition. Then \(T^2-2(\sinh x)T-1=0\).

The roots have product \(-1\). They are \(\frac{4}{7}\) and \(-\frac{7}{4}\) here. Only \(\frac{4}{7}\) is permitted.

extraPractice.title: Use the sign of the logarithm
extraPractice.prompt: Let \(w=\tanh^{-1}\left(-\frac{55}{73}\right)\). Give \(\mathrm e^w\) exactly and identify the sign of \(w\).
extraPractice.hint: Use the principal domain where the original hyperbolic function has an inverse.
extraPractice.solution:
From the tangent definition, \(T^2=\frac{1+\tanh w}{1-\tanh w}\). Use the positive square root for \(T\).

Solving gives \(T=\frac{3}{8}\). The logarithm of \(T\) is negative.

In logarithmic form this evaluation is \(w=\ln\left(\frac{3}{8}\right)\). The argument is positive as required.

glossary.definition: The half-difference of \(\mathrm e^x\) and \(\mathrm e^{-x}\).
The half-sum of the same exponentials.
The ratio of hyperbolic sine to hyperbolic cosine.
The function \(x\mapsto\frac1{f(x)}\) on inputs for which \(f(x)\ne0\).
A root that meets the original domain conditions.

revision.body:
Use the exponential definitions:

\[\begin{aligned}\sinh x&=\frac{\mathrm e^x-\mathrm e^{-x}}{2},\\[2pt]\cosh x&=\frac{\mathrm e^x+\mathrm e^{-x}}{2},\\[2pt]\tanh x&=\frac{\sinh x}{\cosh x}=\frac{\mathrm e^x-\mathrm e^{-x}}{\mathrm e^x+\mathrm e^{-x}}.\end{aligned}\]

Start with \(\cosh x\pm\sinh x=\mathrm e^{\pm x}\). For mixed exponential equations, set \(T=\mathrm e^x>0\). For \(\tanh x=k\), solve linearly in \(U=\mathrm e^{2x}>0\).
revision.checks:
• Can you evaluate the functions when \(\mathrm e^x=\frac32\)?
  • Which reciprocal functions exclude zero?
  • Can the equation \(\tanh x=1\) have a finite solution?
revision.examTip: Reject any negative root for \(T\) explicitly before taking logarithms.

fp2_hyperbolic_graphs.description: Sketch the six hyperbolic curves and locate turning points, asymptotes, symmetry centres and transformed ranges.

sections.title: How can I sketch the three basic curves?
sections.label: Basic graphs
sections.intro: Use the value at zero and symmetry as starting points. The exponential definitions give the behaviour away from zero without a table of many points.

blocks.html: \(\sinh x\) and \(\tanh x\) are odd and both increase through the origin. \(\cosh x\) is even with minimum \((0,1)\). The tangent approaches \(y=\pm1\) while the sine is unbounded.

figure.alt: The two odd curves pass through the origin. Hyperbolic cosine has its minimum at height 1. Hyperbolic tangent stays between the dashed lines at heights −1 and 1.
figure.caption: The two odd curves pass through the origin. Hyperbolic cosine has its minimum at height 1. Hyperbolic tangent stays between the dashed lines at heights −1 and 1.

blocks.html: The curve \(\tanh x\) increases through the origin and levels off away from it. Do not draw it crossing either horizontal asymptote.
For a labelled sketch, include the intercept, turning point or symmetry centre where relevant, plus every asymptote.

blocks.title: Minimum after a shift
blocks.prompt: The function is \(f(x)=3\cosh \bigl(x-1\bigr)+2\). Give the coordinates of the turning point and whether it is a maximum or minimum.
blocks.hint: Locate the argument zero before applying vertical transformations.
blocks.solution:
The input of the hyperbolic cosine is zero at \(x=1\). Its value there is one and all other values are at least one. The vertical multiplier determines which type of turning point remains.

\((1,5)\). Minimum.

blocks.title: Maximum after reflection
blocks.prompt: The function is \(f(x)=-3\cosh \bigl(2(x-4)\bigr)+1\). Give the coordinates of the turning point and whether it is a maximum or minimum.
blocks.hint: Locate the argument zero before applying vertical transformations.
blocks.solution:
The input of the hyperbolic cosine is zero at \(x=4\). Its value there is one and all other values are at least one. The vertical multiplier determines which type of turning point remains.

\((4,-2)\). Maximum.

sections.title: What happens to the minimum of cosh after a transformation?
sections.label: Shift and reflect cosh
sections.intro: The input of the parent curve is zero at its minimum. Find the matching new input and transform the output separately.

blocks.html: For \(a\cosh(b(x-h))+d\) with \(ab\ne0\), the turning point is \((h,a+d)\). It is a minimum for \(a>0\) and a maximum for \(a<0\). The graph is symmetric about \(x=h\).

figure.alt: Dashed parent cosh has its minimum at zero, one. The narrower transformed curve has minimum at three, two.
figure.caption: Compare \(y=\cosh x\) with \(y=3\cosh\bigl(2(x-3)\bigr)-1\). The new minimum is \((3,2)\).

blocks.html: The \(d\) translation is applied after scaling the original minimum of one by \(a\). The new turning height is not generally \(d\).
Check whether the range has a closed endpoint and place the closed bracket on the turning height.

blocks.title: Turning height on the axis
blocks.prompt: The function is \(f(x)=2\cosh \bigl(3(x-3)\bigr)-2\). Give the coordinates of the turning point and whether it is a maximum or minimum.
blocks.hint: Locate the argument zero before applying vertical transformations.
blocks.solution:
The input of the hyperbolic cosine is zero at \(x=3\). Its value there is one and all other values are at least one. The vertical multiplier determines which type of turning point remains.

\((3,0)\). Minimum.

sections.title: Where do the horizontal asymptotes move?
sections.label: Transform tangent limits
sections.intro: The output heights of \(a\tanh(b(x-h))+d\) approach the images of \(-1\) and \(1\). The sign of \(ab\) decides which end approaches which height.

blocks.html: The horizontal asymptote heights are \(d-|a|\) and \(d+|a|\). The centre is \((h,d)\). Neither boundary is attained for a finite input.

figure.alt: Tanh parent has limiting heights negative one and one. Transformed increasing graph has centre one, two and approaches negative one and five.
figure.caption: The centre of \(y=3\tanh\bigl(2(x-1)\bigr)+2\) is \((1,2)\). Its range is \((-1,5)\); neither limit is attained.

blocks.html: A negative \(b\) swaps the two ends but does not change the range. A negative \(a\) also swaps them.
Substitute a large positive input to check the right-hand tail logically.

blocks.title: Order the limiting heights
blocks.prompt: The function is \(f(x)=4\tanh \bigl(2(x-2)\bigr)+3\). Give both horizontal asymptote heights in increasing order and the x-coordinate of the centre of symmetry.
blocks.hint: Locate the argument zero before applying vertical transformations.
blocks.solution:
The hyperbolic tangent stays between \(-1\) and \(1\). The magnitude of the vertical scale sets the two distances from \(3\). The horizontal shift determines the centre.

\(y=-1\) and \(y=7\). The centre is at \(x=2\).

blocks.title: Keep the same range after a horizontal reflection
blocks.prompt: The function is \(f(x)=2\tanh \bigl(-2(x-3)\bigr)+5\). Give both horizontal asymptote heights in increasing order and the x-coordinate of the centre of symmetry.
blocks.hint: Locate the argument zero before applying vertical transformations.
blocks.solution:
The hyperbolic tangent stays between \(-1\) and \(1\). The magnitude of the vertical scale sets the two distances from \(5\). The horizontal shift determines the centre.

\(y=3\) and \(y=7\). The centre is at \(x=3\).

sections.title: How do I locate and orient a transformed sinh graph?
sections.label: Shift the odd curve
sections.intro: An increasing odd curve has a centre where its argument is zero. After a shift, that centre may no longer be on either axis.

blocks.html: \(a\sinh(b(x-h))+d\) is increasing if \(ab>0\) and decreasing if \(ab<0\). Its centre of symmetry is \((h,d)\) and its range remains all real numbers.

figure.alt: Dashed parent sinh increases through zero, zero. The transformed graph decreases through two, four.
figure.caption: Compare \(y=\sinh x\) with \(y=4-\sinh\bigl(3(x-2)\bigr)\). The decreasing curve retains all real output values.

blocks.html: The image of the origin under a transformation is a symmetry centre. It is not automatically a turning point or an intercept.
Compare the transformed graph at inputs equally far either side of \(h\): their heights add to \(2d\).

blocks.title: Two reversals
blocks.prompt: The function is \(f(x)=-2\sinh \bigl(-3(x-1)\bigr)+2\). Give the coordinates of the centre of symmetry and classify the function as increasing or decreasing.
blocks.hint: Locate the argument zero before applying vertical transformations.
blocks.solution:
The centre is where the argument of the original odd function is zero. Reversing one of the horizontal and vertical orientations reverses whether it increases. Reversing both restores the original orientation.

\((1,2)\). Increasing.

sections.title: How do reciprocal graphs inherit restrictions?
sections.label: Reciprocal sketches
sections.intro: Where the denominator approaches zero, its reciprocal can become unbounded. Where the denominator grows without bound, the reciprocal can tend to zero.

blocks.html: \(\operatorname{sech}x\) peaks at \((0,1)\) and tends to \(0\) at both ends. \(\operatorname{cosech}x\) has \(x=0\) as a vertical asymptote and \(y=0\) as a horizontal one. \(\coth x\) also excludes zero, with horizontal limiting heights \(\pm1\).

figure.alt: Only the hyperbolic secant has a point on the vertical axis. The hyperbolic cosecant and cotangent diverge on either side of that axis.
figure.caption: Only the hyperbolic secant has a point on the vertical axis. The hyperbolic cosecant and cotangent diverge on either side of that axis.

blocks.html: Removing an input where the denominator is zero neither removes the entire branch nor creates a zero of the reciprocal.
Take limits from both sides of zero for the two odd reciprocals.

blocks.title: Find both asymptotes
blocks.prompt: What are the asymptotes of \(\operatorname{cosech}x\)?
blocks.hint: Use the behaviour near zero and at both ends.
blocks.solution:
\(\sinh x\to0\) as \(x\to0\), and its magnitude has no upper bound in either direction.

The reciprocal becomes unbounded at zero and tends to zero as the input goes to either infinity.

examples.title: Minimum then translation
examples.question: The function is \(f(x)=2\cosh x+3\). Give the coordinates of the turning point and whether it is a maximum or minimum.
solution: The input of the hyperbolic cosine is zero at \(x=0\). Its value there is one and all other values are at least one. The vertical multiplier determines which type of turning point remains.

examples.title: Reflect and shift
examples.question: The function is \(f(x)=-2\cosh \bigl(x-2\bigr)+1\). Give the coordinates of the turning point and whether it is a maximum or minimum.
solution: The input of the hyperbolic cosine is zero at \(x=2\). Its value there is one and all other values are at least one. The vertical multiplier determines which type of turning point remains.

examples.title: Find zero of the argument
examples.question: The function is \(f(x)=3\cosh \bigl(2(x-3)\bigr)-1\). Give the coordinates of the turning point and whether it is a maximum or minimum.
solution: The input of the hyperbolic cosine is zero at \(x=3\). Its value there is one and all other values are at least one. The vertical multiplier determines which type of turning point remains.

examples.title: Move and scale the limiting heights
examples.question: The function is \(f(x)=3\tanh \bigl(2(x-1)\bigr)+2\). Give both horizontal asymptote heights in increasing order and the x-coordinate of the centre of symmetry.
solution: The hyperbolic tangent stays between \(-1\) and \(1\). The magnitude of the vertical scale sets the two distances from \(2\). The horizontal shift determines the centre.
\(y=-1\) and \(y=5\). The centre is at \(x=1\).

examples.title: Negative scale and two asymptotes
examples.question: The function is \(f(x)=-2\tanh \bigl(-(x-3)\bigr)-4\). Give both horizontal asymptote heights in increasing order and the x-coordinate of the centre of symmetry.
solution: The hyperbolic tangent stays between \(-1\) and \(1\). The magnitude of the vertical scale sets the two distances from \(-4\). The horizontal shift determines the centre.
\(y=-6\) and \(y=-2\). The centre is at \(x=3\).

examples.title: Reverse the orientation once
examples.question: The function is \(f(x)=-\sinh \bigl(3(x-2)\bigr)+4\). Give the coordinates of the centre of symmetry and classify the function as increasing or decreasing.
solution: The centre is where the argument of the original odd function is zero. Reversing one of the horizontal and vertical orientations reverses whether it increases. Reversing both restores the original orientation.
\((2,4)\). Decreasing.

examples.title: Trace a reciprocal curve
examples.question: Which statement describes \(\operatorname{sech}x\)?
solution: The positive denominator \(\cosh x\) is even and has minimum one at zero.
The reciprocal therefore has maximum one there and is defined for all real inputs.

extraPractice.title: Scale the turning height
extraPractice.prompt: The function is \(f(x)=-4\cosh \bigl(x-2\bigr)+3\). Give the coordinates of the turning point and whether it is a maximum or minimum.
extraPractice.hint: Locate the argument zero before applying vertical transformations.
extraPractice.solution:
The input of the hyperbolic cosine is zero at \(x=2\). Its value there is one and all other values are at least one. The vertical multiplier determines which type of turning point remains.

\((2,-1)\). Maximum.

extraPractice.title: Use a fractional scale
extraPractice.prompt: The function is \(f(x)=\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)\tanh\!\left(1(x-3)\right)+\left(4\right)\). Give both horizontal asymptote heights in increasing order and the x-coordinate of the centre of symmetry.
extraPractice.hint: Locate the argument zero before applying vertical transformations.
extraPractice.solution:
The hyperbolic tangent stays between \(-1\) and \(1\). The magnitude of the vertical scale sets the two distances from \(4\). The horizontal shift determines the centre.

\(y=\frac{5}{2}\) and \(y=\frac{11}{2}\). The centre is at \(x=3\).

extraPractice.title: Locate a translated centre
extraPractice.prompt: The function is \(f(x)=3\sinh \bigl(-2(x-4)\bigr)+1\). Give the coordinates of the centre of symmetry and classify the function as increasing or decreasing.
extraPractice.hint: Locate the argument zero before applying vertical transformations.
extraPractice.solution:
The centre is where the argument of the original odd function is zero. Reversing one of the horizontal and vertical orientations reverses whether it increases. Reversing both restores the original orientation.

\((4,1)\). Decreasing.

extraPractice.title: Determine the orientation
extraPractice.prompt: The function is \(f(x)=2\sinh \bigl(2(x-2)\bigr)+5\). Give the coordinates of the centre of symmetry and classify the function as increasing or decreasing.
extraPractice.hint: Locate the argument zero before applying vertical transformations.
extraPractice.solution:
The centre is where the argument of the original odd function is zero. Reversing one of the horizontal and vertical orientations reverses whether it increases. Reversing both restores the original orientation.

\((2,5)\). Increasing.

extraPractice.title: Use the closed turning height
extraPractice.prompt: The function is \(f(x)=\cosh \bigl(4(x-1)\bigr)-2\). Give the coordinates of the turning point and whether it is a maximum or minimum.
extraPractice.hint: Locate the argument zero before applying vertical transformations.
extraPractice.solution:
The input of the hyperbolic cosine is zero at \(x=1\). Its value there is one and all other values are at least one. The vertical multiplier determines which type of turning point remains.

\((1,-1)\). Minimum.

glossary.definition: A function with \(f(-x)=-f(x)\).
A function with \(f(-x)=f(x)\).
A point about which a rotation by \(\pi\) radians preserves the curve.
A limiting horizontal line of an end of the graph.
A local maximum or a local minimum.

revision.body: For \(a\cosh(b(x-h))+d\) use turning point \((h,a+d)\). For \(a\sinh(b(x-h))+d\) and \(a\tanh(b(x-h))+d\) use centre \((h,d)\). The hyperbolic tangent asymptotes have heights \(d\pm|a|\).
revision.checks:
• Is the turning point an upper or lower endpoint of the range?
  • Which limiting height does the tangent approach on the right when \(ab<0\)?
  • Why is \(\operatorname{sech}x\) defined at \(x=0\)?
revision.examTip: An asymptote may give an open range bound. A turning height on the graph is included.

fp2_hyperbolic_identities.description: Prove the fundamental hyperbolic identity, use sum and double-angle formulae and select admissible signs.

sections.title: Why is the difference of the squares always one?
sections.label: The fundamental identity
sections.intro: Expand the sum and difference of reciprocal exponentials. The squares cancel, leaving the cross terms.

blocks.html: \(\cosh^2 x-\sinh^2 x=\frac{(\mathrm e^x+\mathrm e^{-x})^2-(\mathrm e^x-\mathrm e^{-x})^2}{4}=1\). Unlike the ordinary sine and cosine identity, the sign between the squares is a minus.
After using the identity backwards, taking the square root of \(\cosh^2x\) gives \(\cosh x\) because it is positive. The same step for \(\sinh^2x\) gives \(|\sinh x|\).
When you know \(\sinh x\), the sign of any recovered tangent is the same.

blocks.title: Recover an exact positive cosine
blocks.prompt: Given \(\sinh x=\frac{15}{8}\), find \(\cosh x\) and \(\tanh x\).
blocks.hint: Use the identity first. Choose the sign using the information about the input.
blocks.solution:
\(\cosh^2 x=1+\sinh^2 x\); use the positive square root because \(\cosh x\ge1\).

Then \(\tanh x=\frac{\sinh x}{\cosh x}\), which has the same sign as \(\sinh x\).

\(\cosh x=\frac{17}{8}\) and \(\tanh x=\frac{15}{17}\).

blocks.title: Recover the tangent below zero
blocks.prompt: Given \(\sinh x=-\frac{45}{28}\), find \(\cosh x\) and \(\tanh x\).
blocks.hint: Use the identity first. Choose the sign using the information about the input.
blocks.solution:
\(\cosh^2 x=1+\sinh^2 x\); use the positive square root because \(\cosh x\ge1\).

Then \(\tanh x=\frac{\sinh x}{\cosh x}\), which has the same sign as \(\sinh x\).

\(\cosh x=\frac{53}{28}\) and \(\tanh x=-\frac{45}{53}\).

sections.title: Which form is useful when tanh is given?
sections.label: Divide before using
sections.intro: Starting from the fundamental identity, divide by the square of the quantity whose reciprocal you need.

blocks.html: Division by \(\cosh^2x\) gives \(1-\tanh^2x=\operatorname{sech}^2x\). Division by \(\sinh^2x\) for \(x\ne0\) gives \(\coth^2x-1=\operatorname{cosech}^2x\).
The quotient form involving \(\coth x\) is invalid at zero even though the original identity is valid there.
Use the sign of the original quotient to recover the sign of the sine.

blocks.title: Start from the quotient
blocks.prompt: Given \(\tanh x=-\frac{21}{29}\), find \(\cosh x\) and \(\sinh x\).
blocks.hint: Use the identity first. Choose the sign using the information about the input.
blocks.solution:
\(1-\tanh^2x=\operatorname{sech}^2x\); invert this relation and take the positive root for \(\cosh x\).

Multiply that positive value by the specified \(\tanh x\) to obtain \(\sinh x\) with its correct sign.

\(\cosh x=\frac{29}{20}\) and \(\sinh x=-\frac{21}{20}\).

sections.title: How do I decide which square root to take?
sections.label: Sign and completeness
sections.intro: A given cosine value greater than one can come from opposite inputs. A sign restriction on input selects the appropriate value of the sine.

blocks.html: If \(\cosh x=c>1\), then \(\sinh x=\pm\sqrt{c^2-1}\). Keep both signs if \(x\) is unrestricted, otherwise take the sign of \(x\).
Choosing the positive root for \(\sinh x\) by analogy with \(\cosh x\) can drop a valid branch.
Check whether the question asks for a single branch, all values or a proof.

blocks.title: Use the given sign
blocks.prompt: Given \(\cosh x=\frac{5}{4},\quad x<0\), find \(\sinh x\) and \(\tanh x\).
blocks.hint: Use the identity first. Choose the sign using the information about the input.
blocks.solution:
\(\sinh^2x=\cosh^2x-1\). The sign of \(\sinh x\) agrees with the sign of \(x\).

Divide the selected signed square root by \(\cosh x\) to obtain \(\tanh x\).

\(\sinh x=-\frac{3}{4}\) and \(\tanh x=-\frac{3}{5}\).

blocks.title: Retain both reciprocal roots
blocks.prompt: Solve \(\cosh x=\frac{13}{5}\). Give every value of \(T=\mathrm e^x\).
blocks.hint: No restriction was placed on the input of cosh.
blocks.solution:
The substitution gives \(T+\frac1T=\frac{26}{5}\) and therefore \(T^2-\frac{26}{5}T+1=0\).

The quadratic has reciprocal positive roots \(\frac{1}{5}\) and \(5\). Both are admissible for the equation. The two values of \(x\) are opposite logarithms.

sections.title: How do sum identities follow from exponentials?
sections.label: Sum of arguments
sections.intro: Use \(\mathrm e^{x+y}=\mathrm e^x\mathrm e^y\) and the corresponding identity for the negative exponent. Add or subtract the expanded products.

blocks.html: \(\sinh(x+y)=\sinh x\cosh y+\cosh x\sinh y\) and \(\cosh(x+y)=\cosh x\cosh y+\sinh x\sinh y\). Replacing \(y\) by \(-y\) gives the subtraction formulae.
In the cosine addition formula both products are added. The hyperbolic sine of a negative input can still make the second product negative.
Recover the exponential of the sum from the two calculated values as a check.

blocks.title: Check the product exponent
blocks.prompt: Given \(\mathrm e^x=\frac{3}{2}\) and \(\mathrm e^y=\frac{1}{4}\), give \(\sinh(x+y)\) and \(\cosh(x+y)\) exactly.
blocks.hint: Check the sign in the hyperbolic cosine addition formula.
blocks.solution:
Use \(\sinh(x+y)=\sinh x\cosh y+\cosh x\sinh y\) for the first value and \(\cosh(x+y)=\cosh x\cosh y+\sinh x\sinh y\) for the second.

As a check, substitute \(\mathrm e^{x+y}=\frac{3}{8}\) in the definitions.

\(-\frac{55}{48}\) and \(\frac{73}{48}\), respectively.

sections.title: When does a double argument simplify the equation?
sections.label: Double-angle identities
sections.intro: Set \(y=x\) in the addition formulae. For cosine, there are three equivalent forms, so match the one that uses the quantity you already know.

blocks.html: \(\sinh 2x=2\sinh x\cosh x\) and \(\cosh 2x=\cosh^2x+\sinh^2x=1+2\sinh^2x=2\cosh^2x-1\).
\(\cosh 2x\) is always at least one. A rearranged expression below this bound immediately flags a sign error.
If an equation is quadratic in \(\cosh x\), retain only values of that variable that are at least one.

blocks.title: Check the sign of the doubled sine
blocks.prompt: Given \(\mathrm e^x=\frac{1}{3}\), give \(\sinh 2x\) and \(\cosh 2x\) exactly.

fp2_hyperbolic_inverse.description: Find the domains and ranges of the inverse hyperbolic functions and explain the principal branch of inverse cosh.

sections.title: Which hyperbolic graphs can be inverted as they stand?
sections.label: When an inverse exists
sections.intro: An inverse must give a unique input for each output. Use the horizontal-line test on the function you want to reverse.

blocks.html: \(\sinh\) and \(\tanh\) are strictly increasing on \(\mathbb R\). The inverse of \(\sinh\) takes all real inputs, whereas \(\tanh^{-1}\) accepts only \(-1
An asymptote height is not part of the range of \(\tanh\), so it cannot be an input to its inverse.
Say which original range supplies the inverse domain.

blocks.title: Read the allowed inputs after a shift
blocks.prompt: What is the domain of \(\sinh^{-1}(x-3)\)?
blocks.hint: Check what the unshifted inverse can accept.
blocks.solution:
The inverse sine accepts every real input because \(\sinh\) attains all real values.

Subtracting three from a real number keeps the argument real and imposes no extra restriction.

blocks.title: Transform an open inverse domain
blocks.prompt: What is the domain of \(\tanh^{-1}(2x-1)\)?
blocks.hint: Use the full argument \(2x-1\) in the domain condition.
blocks.solution:
The inner argument must satisfy \(-1<2x-1<1\).

Add one, then halve every part. Both endpoints remain excluded.

sections.title: Why does inverse cosh use the non-negative branch?
sections.label: Restrict the even curve
sections.intro: The unreduced curve has a left and a right input with the same height. Standard notation selects the right-hand input as the principal value.

blocks.html: Cosh is restricted to \(x\ge0\) before inversion. Thus \(\cosh^{-1}x\) has domain \(x\ge1\) and range \(y\ge0\).
Using both input signs for a value of \(\cosh^{-1}x\) makes it no longer a function.
An equation \(\cosh x=c\) without a domain restriction can still have two roots; it asks a different question.

blocks.title: Select the branch at a different height
blocks.prompt: Let \(w=\cosh^{-1}\left(\frac{13}{12}\right)\). Give \(\mathrm e^w\) exactly and identify the sign of \(w\).
blocks.hint: Use the principal domain where the original hyperbolic function has an inverse.
blocks.solution:
The cosine equation gives \(T^2-2(\frac{13}{12})T+1=0\). The principal branch has \(w\ge0\) and thus \(T\ge1\).

Solving gives \(T=\frac{3}{2}\). The logarithm of \(T\) is positive.

sections.title: What does the reflected graph tell me?
sections.label: Reflect across y = x
sections.intro: Reflecting a point \((u,v)\) on the chosen original branch gives \((v,u)\) on the inverse. Horizontal and vertical features are interchanged.

blocks.html: The endpoint \((0,1)\) of restricted \(\cosh\) becomes \((1,0)\) on its inverse. The two horizontal asymptotes of \(\tanh\) become vertical lines \(x=\pm1\).

figure.alt: The restricted curve starts at (0, 1). Its reflected inverse starts at (1, 0). The dashed line is the diagonal of reflection.
figure.caption: The restricted curve starts at (0, 1). Its reflected inverse starts at (1, 0). The dashed line is the diagonal of reflection.

blocks.html: Reflect only the chosen branch of cosh. Reflecting the entire U shape gives a relation with two outputs.
Label the original and inverse endpoint coordinates before drawing curves.

blocks.title: Move the inverse cosine range
blocks.prompt: What is the range of \(3+\cosh^{-1}x\)?
blocks.hint: Apply the translation to output heights.
blocks.solution:
The range of the principal inverse is \([0,\infty)\).

Adding three to each output raises the endpoint to three and preserves all greater outputs.

blocks.title: Locate both reflected asymptotes
blocks.prompt: Which vertical asymptotes belong to \(y=\tanh^{-1}(x-2)\)?
blocks.hint: Translate each input where the original inverse approaches a vertical asymptote.
blocks.solution:
The original inverse tangent has vertical asymptotes at inputs \(-1\) and \(1\).

Set \(x-2=-1\) and \(x-2=1\) to find the translated positions.

sections.title: When does composing an inverse give the original input?
sections.label: Check both compositions
sections.intro: One composition starts on the inverse domain, the other on the selected original branch. On restricted cosh this difference matters.

blocks.html: \(\cosh(\cosh^{-1}y)=y\) for \(y\ge1\). For arbitrary real \(x\), \(\cosh^{-1}(\cosh x)=|x|\), with the absolute value choosing the non-negative input.
Writing \(\cosh^{-1}(\cosh(-2))=-2\) conflicts with the range of inverse cosh.
Always check the domain before cancelling a function with its inverse.

blocks.title: Use the right-hand preimage
blocks.prompt: Evaluate \(\cosh^{-1}\left(\cosh(-5)\right)\).
blocks.hint: Check which side of zero is selected in the definition of the inverse.
blocks.solution:
The input of the inverse is a height of the even function. On the positive branch the same height occurs at \(5\).

The principal output is \(5\).

sections.title: What if the original equation allows both roots?
sections.label: Inverse value versus equation
sections.intro: An inverse result can give one root of an equation. Use the symmetry of the original function to determine whether there is another.

blocks.html: If \(k>1\), \(\cosh x=k\) has solutions \(\pm\cosh^{-1}k\). For \(k=1\) they coincide at zero. For \(k<1\) there are no real solutions.
A single principal value is sufficient for \(\cosh^{-1}k\), but it is incomplete when asked to solve \(\cosh x=k>1\).
Determine whether you are evaluating a function or finding all preimages.

blocks.title: Find both admissible exponentials
blocks.prompt: Solve \(\cosh x=\frac{5}{4}\). Give every value of \(T=\mathrm e^x\).
blocks.hint: No restriction was placed on the input of cosh.
blocks.solution:
The substitution gives \(T+\frac1T=\frac{5}{2}\) and therefore \(T^2-\frac{5}{2}T+1=0\).

The quadratic has reciprocal positive roots \(\frac{1}{2}\) and \(2\). Both are admissible for the equation. The two values of \(x\) are opposite logarithms.

examples.title: The inverse tangent domain
examples.question: Which set is the domain of \(\tanh^{-1}\)?
solution: \(\tanh\) is strictly increasing through zero and approaches but never reaches one or negative one.
The inverse takes as its inputs the values produced by the chosen original branch.

examples.title: The inverse sine domain
examples.question: Which set is the domain of \(\sinh^{-1}\)?
solution: \(\sinh\) is strictly increasing through zero.
The inverse takes as its inputs the values produced by the chosen original branch.

examples.title: Select the principal cosine branch
examples.question: Let \(w=\cosh^{-1}\left(\frac{5}{3}\right)\). Give \(\mathrm e^w\) exactly and identify the sign of \(w\).
solution: The cosine equation gives \(T^2-2(\frac{5}{3})T+1=0\). The principal branch has \(w\ge0\) and thus \(T\ge1\).
Solving gives \(T=3\). The logarithm of \(T\) is positive.
In logarithmic form this evaluation is \(w=\ln\left(3\right)\). The argument is positive as required.

examples.title: The reflected cosine endpoint
examples.question: Which set is the range of \(\cosh^{-1}\)?
solution: Restrict the original \(\cosh\) to \(x\ge0\). It is increasing from one on this branch.
The outputs of the inverse are precisely the inputs of the chosen original branch.

examples.title: The range after reflection
examples.question: Which set is the range of \(\tanh^{-1}\)?
solution: \(\tanh\) is strictly increasing through zero and approaches but never reaches one or negative one.
The outputs of the inverse are precisely the inputs of the chosen original branch.

examples.title: Compose with a negative input
examples.question: Evaluate \(\cosh^{-1}\left(\cosh(-3)\right)\).
solution: The input of the inverse is a height of the even function. On the positive branch the same height occurs at \(3\).
The principal output is \(3\).

examples.title: A cosine equation uses both signs
examples.question: Solve \(\cosh x=\frac{5}{3}\). Give every value of \(T=\mathrm e^x\).
solution: The substitution gives \(T+\frac1T=\frac{10}{3}\) and therefore \(T^2-\frac{10}{3}T+1=0\).
The quadratic has reciprocal positive roots \(\frac{1}{3}\) and \(3\). Both are admissible for the equation. The two values of \(x\) are opposite logarithms.

extraPractice.prompt: Which set is the domain of \(\cosh^{-1}\)?
extraPractice.hint: Original range becomes inverse domain.
extraPractice.solution:
Restrict the original \(\cosh\) to \(x\ge0\). It is increasing from one on this branch.

The inverse takes as its inputs the values produced by the chosen original branch.

extraPractice.prompt: Evaluate \(\cosh^{-1}\left(\cosh(0)\right)\).
extraPractice.hint: Check which side of zero is selected in the definition of the inverse.
extraPractice.solution:
The input of the inverse is a height of the even function. On the positive branch the same height occurs at \(0\).

The principal output is \(0\).

extraPractice.hint: Check which side of zero is selected in the definition of the inverse.
extraPractice.solution:

extraPractice.prompt: Let \(w=\tanh^{-1}\left(-\frac{5}{13}\right)\). Give \(\mathrm e^w\) exactly and identify the sign of \(w\).
extraPractice.hint: Use the principal domain where the original hyperbolic function has an inverse.
extraPractice.solution:
From the tangent definition, \(T^2=\frac{1+\tanh w}{1-\tanh w}\). Use the positive square root for \(T\).

Solving gives \(T=\frac{2}{3}\). The logarithm of \(T\) is negative.

extraPractice.title: Keep both roots of the unrestricted equation
extraPractice.prompt: Solve \(\cosh x=\frac{37}{12}\). Give every value of \(T=\mathrm e^x\).
extraPractice.hint: No restriction was placed on the input of cosh.
extraPractice.solution:
The substitution gives \(T+\frac1T=\frac{37}{6}\) and therefore \(T^2-\frac{37}{6}T+1=0\).

The quadratic has reciprocal positive roots \(\frac{1}{6}\) and \(6\). Both are admissible for the equation. The two values of \(x\) are opposite logarithms.

fp2_hyperbolic_logarithms.description: Derive the logarithmic forms of inverse sinh, cosh and tanh, then simplify exact inverse expressions.

sections.title: How do I derive the logarithm for inverse sinh?
sections.label: Derive inverse sinh
sections.intro: Set \(w=\sinh^{-1}x\) and \(T=\mathrm e^w>0\). Reversing the inverse statement gives \(2x=T-\frac1T\).

blocks.html: The quadratic \(T^2-2xT-1=0\) has roots \(x\pm\sqrt{x^2+1}\). Since \(\sqrt{x^2+1}>|x|\), only the plus root is positive. Hence \(\sinh^{-1}x=\ln(x+\sqrt{x^2+1})\) for all real \(x\).
For negative \(x\), the plus sign is still required. The magnitude of the square root is strictly greater than \(|x|\).
Justify positivity from the inequality, even if the formula is supplied.

blocks.title: Use the positive root of a quadratic
blocks.prompt: Let \(w=\sinh^{-1}\left(-\frac{15}{8}\right)\). Give \(\mathrm e^w\) exactly and identify the sign of \(w\).
blocks.hint: Use the principal domain where the original hyperbolic function has an inverse.
blocks.solution:
Write \(T=\mathrm e^w>0\). The sine equation gives \(T^2-2(-\frac{15}{8})T-1=0\). The other root has opposite sign.

Solving gives \(T=\frac{1}{4}\). The logarithm of \(T\) is negative.

In logarithmic form this evaluation is \(w=\ln\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)\). The argument is positive as required.

blocks.title: At the start of the cosine branch
blocks.prompt: Let \(w=\cosh^{-1}\left(1\right)\). Give \(\mathrm e^w\) exactly and identify the sign of \(w\).
blocks.hint: Use the principal domain where the original hyperbolic function has an inverse.
blocks.solution:
The cosine equation gives \(T^2-2(1)T+1=0\). The principal branch has \(w\ge0\) and thus \(T\ge1\).

Solving gives \(T=1\). The logarithm of \(T\) is zero.

In logarithmic form this evaluation is \(w=\ln\left(1\right)\). The argument is positive as required.

sections.title: Why is positivity alone not enough for inverse cosh?
sections.label: Derive inverse cosh
sections.intro: Set \(w=\cosh^{-1}x\). Now both candidate exponentials can be positive because their product is one.

blocks.html: The equation \(T^2-2xT+1=0\) gives \(T=x\pm\sqrt{x^2-1}\) for \(x\ge1\). The principal restriction \(w\ge0\) requires \(T\ge1\). Thus \(\cosh^{-1}x=\ln(x+\sqrt{x^2-1})\).
Discarding the smaller root because it is negative is wrong. It is positive and less than one when \(x>1\).
When \(x=1\), the roots coincide and yield \(\ln1=0\).

blocks.title: Return from a positive quotient
blocks.prompt: Let \(w=\tanh^{-1}\left(\frac{5}{13}\right)\). Give \(\mathrm e^w\) exactly and identify the sign of \(w\).
blocks.hint: Use the principal domain where the original hyperbolic function has an inverse.
blocks.solution:
From the tangent definition, \(T^2=\frac{1+\tanh w}{1-\tanh w}\). Use the positive square root for \(T\).

Solving gives \(T=\frac{3}{2}\). The logarithm of \(T\) is positive.

In logarithmic form this evaluation is \(w=\ln\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)\). The argument is positive as required.

sections.title: Why is there a half in the logarithm for inverse tanh?
sections.label: Derive inverse tanh
sections.intro: The quotient contains twice the unknown in the exponent, so the transformed equation is linear for \(U=\mathrm e^{2w}\).

blocks.html: From \(x=\frac{U-1}{U+1}\) obtain \(U=\frac{1+x}{1-x}\). Both numerator and denominator are positive for \(|x|<1\). Consequently \(\tanh^{-1}x=\frac12\ln\!\left(\frac{1+x}{1-x}\right)\).
If you take \(\ln U\) and stop, you have found \(2w\).
At \(x=0\) the logarithm is \(\ln1\), which checks the formula.

blocks.title: Multiply two rational arguments

examples.title: Derive the plus root for a negative input
examples.question: Let \(w=\sinh^{-1}\left(-\frac{4}{3}\right)\). Give \(\mathrm e^w\) exactly and identify the sign of \(w\).

fp2_hyperbolic_mixed.description: Combine hyperbolic functions into a quadratic in a positive variable and count intersections by comparing levels.

sections.title: Which substitution matches the given expression?
sections.label: Choose a method
sections.intro: First identify whether one function, a squared function, a pair of reciprocal exponentials or a quotient is responsible for the unknown.

blocks.html: Use an inverse for one function, a hyperbolic identity for related squares, \(T=\mathrm e^x>0\) for a linear combination of \(\sinh x\) and \(\cosh x\), and \(U=\mathrm e^{2x}\) for the quotient \(\tanh x\).
Expanding every term in exponentials can create a higher-degree equation. Simplify the argument structure before choosing the substitution.
Write the range restriction for the transformed unknown next to its definition.

blocks.title: Reduce to a quadratic
blocks.prompt: Solve \(5\cosh x+\left(3\right)\sinh x=\frac{37}{3}\) by substituting \(T=\mathrm e^x\). Give the complete set of positive values of \(T\).
blocks.hint: Collect the two exponential terms before solving the quadratic. Enforce positivity at the end.
blocks.solution:
Expand the definitions to get \(4T+\frac{1}T=\frac{37}{3}\). Multiply by the positive variable \(T\).

The resulting quadratic has candidate roots \(3\) and \(\frac{1}{12}\). Retain the positive candidates and count a repeated candidate once.

The complete transformed set is \(\left\{\frac{1}{12},3\right\}\). The corresponding values of \(x\) are the logarithms of its members.

blocks.title: Recognise the mixed-sign coefficients
blocks.prompt: Solve \(2\cosh x+\left(5\right)\sinh x=\frac{17}{4}\) by substituting \(T=\mathrm e^x\). Give the complete set of positive values of \(T\).
blocks.hint: Collect the two exponential terms before solving the quadratic. Enforce positivity at the end.
blocks.solution:
Expand the definitions to get \(\frac{7}{2}T+\frac{-\frac{3}{2}}T=\frac{17}{4}\). Multiply by the positive variable \(T\).

The resulting quadratic has candidate roots \(\frac{3}{2}\) and \(-\frac{2}{7}\). Retain the positive candidates and count a repeated candidate once.

The complete transformed set is \(\left\{\frac{3}{2}\right\}\). The corresponding values of \(x\) are the logarithms of its members.

sections.title: How do I reduce a linear combination to a quadratic?
sections.label: Combine exponentials
sections.intro: Collect terms in \(T\) and in \(\frac1T\). The coefficients of the two terms need not have the same sign.

blocks.html: \(A\cosh x+B\sinh x=\frac{A+B}{2}T+\frac{A-B}{2T}\). Multiplying by \(2T\) turns an equation with right side \(k\) into \((A+B)T^2-2kT+(A-B)=0\).
If one of \(A+B\) or \(A-B\) is zero, simplify the resulting equation while retaining \(T>0\). A formal root at zero is excluded.
Convert every retained positive root to \(\ln T\).

blocks.title: Collect two fractional terms
blocks.prompt: Solve \(8\cosh x+\left(2\right)\sinh x=\frac{31}{4}\) by substituting \(T=\mathrm e^x\). Give the complete set of positive values of \(T\).
blocks.hint: Collect the two exponential terms before solving the quadratic. Enforce positivity at the end.
blocks.solution:
Expand the definitions to get \(5T+\frac{3}T=\frac{31}{4}\). Multiply by the positive variable \(T\).

The resulting quadratic has candidate roots \(\frac{3}{4}\) and \(\frac{4}{5}\). Retain the positive candidates and count a repeated candidate once.

The complete transformed set is \(\left\{\frac{3}{4},\frac{4}{5}\right\}\). The corresponding values of \(x\) are the logarithms of its members.

sections.title: When can there be two valid logarithms?
sections.label: Retain all positive roots
sections.intro: After collecting a sum \(aT+\frac bT\), look for independent positive roots. They need not be reciprocal unless the coefficients match.

blocks.html: For \(a,b>0\), a root \(T\) of \(aT^2-kT+b=0\) is accompanied by \(\frac{b}{aT}\). Both are positive. They coincide only when \(T^2=\frac ba\).
Opposite signs of the two exponents in the original functions do not guarantee opposite values of \(x\).
Check the product of the quadratic roots before deciding which roots to keep.

blocks.title: Find two positive roots
blocks.prompt: Solve \(6\cosh x+\left(-2\right)\sinh x=\frac{22}{3}\) by substituting \(T=\mathrm e^x\). Give the complete set of positive values of \(T\).
blocks.hint: Collect the two exponential terms before solving the quadratic. Enforce positivity at the end.
blocks.solution:
Expand the definitions to get \(2T+\frac{4}T=\frac{22}{3}\). Multiply by the positive variable \(T\).

The resulting quadratic has candidate roots \(3\) and \(\frac{2}{3}\). Retain the positive candidates and count a repeated candidate once.

The complete transformed set is \(\left\{\frac{2}{3},3\right\}\). The corresponding values of \(x\) are the logarithms of its members.

blocks.title: Verify the product of roots
blocks.prompt: Solve \(5\cosh x+\left(1\right)\sinh x=\frac{155}{14}\) by substituting \(T=\mathrm e^x\). Give the complete set of positive values of \(T\).
blocks.hint: Collect the two exponential terms before solving the quadratic. Enforce positivity at the end.
blocks.solution:
Expand the definitions to get \(3T+\frac{2}T=\frac{155}{14}\). Multiply by the positive variable \(T\).

The resulting quadratic has candidate roots \(\frac{7}{2}\) and \(\frac{4}{21}\). Retain the positive candidates and count a repeated candidate once.

The complete transformed set is \(\left\{\frac{4}{21},\frac{7}{2}\right\}\). The corresponding values of \(x\) are the logarithms of its members.

sections.title: When must a quadratic root be discarded?
sections.label: Discard inadmissible values
sections.intro: A positive root yields a real logarithm, a negative root does not. Two roots in the algebra can therefore give only one possible real argument.

blocks.html: If \(ab<0\) in \(aT^2-kT+b=0\), the product of the roots is negative. Exactly one root is positive and it gives the whole real solution.
Taking an absolute value inside the logarithm silently introduces a false solution.
Test the surviving value directly in \(aT+\frac bT\).

blocks.title: Remove the negative candidate
blocks.prompt: Solve \(2\cosh x+\left(4\right)\sinh x=\frac{26}{3}\) by substituting \(T=\mathrm e^x\). Give the complete set of positive values of \(T\).
blocks.hint: Collect the two exponential terms before solving the quadratic. Enforce positivity at the end.
blocks.solution:
Expand the definitions to get \(3T+\frac{-1}T=\frac{26}{3}\). Multiply by the positive variable \(T\).

The resulting quadratic has candidate roots \(3\) and \(-\frac{1}{9}\). Retain the positive candidates and count a repeated candidate once.

The complete transformed set is \(\left\{3\right\}\). The corresponding values of \(x\) are the logarithms of its members.

sections.title: How many solutions are possible before any exact solving?
sections.label: Count the intersection
sections.intro: For \(a,b>0\), the positive variable \(T\) can trade off a term increasing with \(T\) against one decreasing with \(T\).

blocks.html: For \(T>0\), \(aT+\frac bT\ge2\sqrt{ab}\), with equality exactly at \(T=\sqrt{\frac ba}\). The quadratic discriminant gives two distinct positive roots when \(k>2\sqrt{ab}\); none exist below the minimum.

blocks.html: For \(k<-2\sqrt{ab}\) the quadratic has real roots but both are negative. A positive discriminant on its own is insufficient.
Use the allowed values of \(T\) before drawing conclusions from a discriminant.

blocks.title: Count two positive intersections
blocks.prompt: For \(T>0\), how many solutions does \(2T+\frac{8}{T}=9\) have?
blocks.hint: Compare with the minimum and check the positivity of T.
blocks.solution:
Since \(T>0\), the minimum is \(2\sqrt{ab}=8\). The equality case has \(T=\sqrt{\frac ba}\).

Compare the level \(9\) with that minimum. If it is above the minimum, the positive discriminant together with positive sum and product gives two positive roots.

Here the number of admissible roots is \(2\).

examples.title: Choose a positive exponential
examples.question: Solve \(5\cosh x+\left(3\right)\sinh x=\frac{17}{2}\) by substituting \(T=\mathrm e^x\). Give the complete set of positive values of \(T\).
solution: Expand the definitions to get \(4T+\frac{1}T=\frac{17}{2}\). Multiply by the positive variable \(T\).
The resulting quadratic has candidate roots \(2\) and \(\frac{1}{8}\). Retain the positive candidates and count a repeated candidate once.
The complete transformed set is \(\left\{\frac{1}{8},2\right\}\). The corresponding values of \(x\) are the logarithms of its members.

solution: Expand the definitions to get \(\frac{7}{2}T+\frac{-\frac{3}{2}}T=10\). Multiply by the positive variable \(T\).
The resulting quadratic has candidate roots \(3\) and \(-\frac{1}{7}\). Retain the positive candidates and count a repeated candidate once.
The complete transformed set is \(\left\{3\right\}\). The corresponding values of \(x\) are the logarithms of its members.

examples.title: Collect a pair of coefficients

solution: Expand the definitions to get \(3T+\frac{2}T=5\). Multiply by the positive variable \(T\).
The resulting quadratic has candidate roots \(\frac{2}{3}\) and \(1\). Retain the positive candidates and count a repeated candidate once.
The complete transformed set is \(\left\{\frac{2}{3},1\right\}\). The corresponding values of \(x\) are the logarithms of its members.

examples.title: Retain two positive candidates
examples.question: Solve \(5\cosh x+\left(-1\right)\sinh x=\frac{35}{4}\) by substituting \(T=\mathrm e^x\). Give the complete set of positive values of \(T\).
solution: Expand the definitions to get \(2T+\frac{3}T=\frac{35}{4}\). Multiply by the positive variable \(T\).
The resulting quadratic has candidate roots \(4\) and \(\frac{3}{8}\). Retain the positive candidates and count a repeated candidate once.
The complete transformed set is \(\left\{\frac{3}{8},4\right\}\). The corresponding values of \(x\) are the logarithms of its members.

examples.title: Identify unequal opposite exponents
examples.question: Solve \(7\cosh x+\left(3\right)\sinh x=\frac{133}{10}\) by substituting \(T=\mathrm e^x\). Give the complete set of positive values of \(T\).
solution: Expand the definitions to get \(5T+\frac{2}T=\frac{133}{10}\). Multiply by the positive variable \(T\).
The resulting quadratic has candidate roots \(\frac{5}{2}\) and \(\frac{4}{25}\). Retain the positive candidates and count a repeated candidate once.
The complete transformed set is \(\left\{\frac{4}{25},\frac{5}{2}\right\}\). The corresponding values of \(x\) are the logarithms of its members.

examples.title: Reject the negative candidate
examples.question: Solve \(\cosh x+\left(3\right)\sinh x=\frac{7}{2}\) by substituting \(T=\mathrm e^x\). Give the complete set of positive values of \(T\).
solution: Expand the definitions to get \(2T+\frac{-1}T=\frac{7}{2}\). Multiply by the positive variable \(T\).
The resulting quadratic has candidate roots \(2\) and \(-\frac{1}{4}\). Retain the positive candidates and count a repeated candidate once.
The complete transformed set is \(\left\{2\right\}\). The corresponding values of \(x\) are the logarithms of its members.

examples.title: Analyse a repeated positive root
examples.question: For \(T>0\), how many solutions does \(T+\frac{9}{T}=6\) have?
solution: Since \(T>0\), the minimum is \(2\sqrt{ab}=6\). The equality case has \(T=\sqrt{\frac ba}\).
Compare the level \(6\) with that minimum. If it is above the minimum, the positive discriminant together with positive sum and product gives two positive roots.
Here the number of admissible roots is \(1\).

extraPractice.hint: Compare with the minimum and check the positivity of T.
